The NYPSC also has a defined role to identify additional benefit criteria that will be used for project selection. 3.3.2 Cost Allocation Method Design The design of the cost allocation method itself will determine the cost responsibility among network users. Three lessons in method design were identified: 1. Simple methods that can identify project beneficiaries but do not require detailed power system modeling can improve consistency and predictability in cost allocation outcomes, reduce cost allocation disputes, and strike a balance in method usability and accuracy. As discussed in Section 2.2, methods that consider network usage a proxy for benefits are the most common approach for cost allocation. Among the case studies, MISO, SPP, and ISO-NE all use a form of load ratio share to approximate network usage and to allocate costs. The benefit of using load ratio share is the calculation does not require power system modeling and cost allocation is not strictly based on calculated benefits, which can reduce disputes over study assumptions and benefit metrics. Rather, input data on load forecasts or historic load can be readily obtained to validate and predict cost allocation outcomes. In addition, the approach is flexible and can be implemented in different ways, including allowing for regular updates to reflect changing system conditions. For example, ISO-NE uses monthly peak demand, MISO uses monthly energy use, and ERCOT focuses on peak demand during the summer months. PJM’s Artificial Island Project illustrates some of the challenges using a more complex cost allocation approach. The DFAX and stability deviation methods used by PJM require power system modeling to determine each zone or customer’s contribution to power flows or angle deviations, respectively. As seen in the case study, the results are sensitive to the modeling assumptions and type of model used, reducing the consistency and predictability of the results. In addition, quantifying different types of transmission benefits with detailed modeling may require a range of power system models, increasing the complexity and effort required. The JTIQ and the NYISO’s AC Transmission Needs projects combine simple and complex methods. Similar to most generator interconnection projects, the JTIQ portfolio is funded primarily by interconnection customers with 10% of the capital cost originally allocated to load. Although the cost share to load is small, it requires not only production cost modeling to assess the economic benefits to each region but agreement between SPP and MISO on modeling assumptions and methods to reach a common solution. Similarly, the NYISO’s AC Transmission Needs project used a combination of quantified economic benefits and load ratio share.
